records.citation: Garber CE, et al. Quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(7):1334-1359.
records.population: Apparently healthy adults receiving general exercise prescription guidance.
records.limitations: Population guidance from 2011; it does not determine an individual's starting dose or validate a SportRX program pack.

records.citation: Currier BS, et al. ACSM Position Stand: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(4):851-872.
records.population: Healthy adults aged 18 years or older in resistance-training reviews of at least six weeks.
records.limitations: An overview of reviews supports population-level prescription principles; it is not a beginner-specific SportRX starting algorithm or a guarantee of individual response.

records.citation: Currier BS, et al. Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(18):1211-1220.
records.population: Healthy adults in randomized resistance-training trials.
records.limitations: Network rankings compare study prescriptions and should not be treated as a universal best program for every trainee.

records.citation: Grgic J, et al. Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sport Health Sci. 2022;11(2):202-211.
records.population: Predominantly young adults in resistance-training intervention studies.
records.limitations: The evidence base was small and concentrated in young adults; it does not establish one optimal proximity-to-failure target for every exercise or user.

records.citation: Refalo MC, et al. Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(3):649-665.
records.population: Healthy adults across ages and resistance-training experience where hypertrophy was measured.
records.limitations: Definitions of failure and non-failure varied, and the review does not validate a universal RIR threshold.

records.citation: Robinson ZP, et al. Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions. Sports Med. 2024;54(9):2209-2231.
records.population: Healthy adults in longitudinal resistance-training studies reporting estimated repetitions in reserve.
records.limitations: RIR was estimated retrospectively across heterogeneous studies; the analysis does not establish precise personal cutoffs or prove user-reported RIR accuracy.

records.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, et al. How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? J Sports Sci. 2019;37(11):1286-1295.
records.population: Adults in resistance-training frequency studies measuring hypertrophy.
records.limitations: Frequency effects are difficult to separate from volume; findings do not require one fixed weekly split.

records.citation: Androulakis-Korakakis P, et al. The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required to Increase 1RM Strength in Resistance-Trained Men. Sports Med. 2020;50(4):751-765.
records.population: Resistance-trained men, primarily squat and bench-press studies.
records.limitations: Only six studies, trained men, and narrow lifts; the reported dose was explicitly suboptimal and is not a general beginner prescription.

records.citation: Schumann M, et al. Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function. Sports Med. 2022;52(3):601-612.
records.population: Healthy adults completing supervised concurrent aerobic and strength training for at least four weeks.
records.limitations: Group-level findings do not determine an individual's weekly schedule; explosive-strength effects require attention to session timing and context.

records.citation: Wen D, et al. Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults. J Sci Med Sport. 2019;22(8):941-947.
records.population: Healthy, overweight or obese, and athletic adults in randomized HIIT studies.
records.limitations: Protocols and populations were heterogeneous; efficacy findings do not make HIIT an appropriate default for every user.

records.citation: Rosenblat MA, et al. Risk of bias and reporting practices in studies comparing VO2max responses to sprint interval vs continuous training. J Sport Health Sci. 2022;11(5):552-566.
records.population: Healthy adults in supervised sprint-interval and moderate-continuous training studies.
records.limitations: Included studies had unclear risk of bias and poor reporting; apparent equivalence must be interpreted cautiously.

records.citation: Jayedi A, et al. Aerobic Exercise and Weight Loss in Adults: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis. JAMA Netw Open. 2024;7(12):e2452185.
records.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in supervised aerobic-training randomized trials lasting at least eight weeks.
records.limitations: Average trial effects do not predict individual weight loss; the evidence is specific to adults with overweight or obesity and supervised interventions.

records.citation: Oppert JM, et al. Exercise training in the management of overweight and obesity in adults: EASO evidence synthesis and recommendations. Obes Rev. 2021;22 Suppl 4:e13273.
records.limitations: Obesity-management recommendations are not a general-population guarantee, nutrition plan, or individualized medical treatment pathway.

records.citation: Armstrong A, et al. Effect of aerobic exercise on waist circumference in adults with overweight or obesity. Obes Rev. 2022;23(8):e13446.
records.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in randomized aerobic-exercise trials.
records.limitations: Average waist changes cannot be promised to an individual, and measurement conditions must be kept consistent for personal tracking.

records.citation: Chen X, et al. Effects of various exercise types on visceral adipose tissue in individuals with overweight and obesity. Obes Rev. 2024;25(3):e13666.
records.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in randomized exercise trials.
records.limitations: Network comparisons across heterogeneous interventions do not identify one universally superior personal program.

records.citation: Binmahfoz A, et al. Effect of resistance exercise during dietary weight loss in people living with overweight or obesity. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2025;11(3):e002363.
records.population: Adults aged 18-65 years with overweight or obesity undertaking dietary weight loss.
records.limitations: The comparison includes dietary interventions outside SportRX's current product scope; it cannot be converted into a nutrition prescription or guaranteed body-composition result.

records.citation: Streb AR, et al. Characteristics of interventions with exercise according to the adherence of adults with obesity: a systematic review. Clin Obes. 2025;15(3):e12733.
records.population: Adults with obesity in exercise intervention studies.
records.limitations: Adherence ranged widely and intervention components were heterogeneous; associations do not prove that any one feature will improve an individual's adherence.
